title.en: The Woman and the Eel at the Suqe Oven
title.zh: 婦人與鰻：蘇蓋爐中食鰻之禍

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A woman's soaking pandanus leaves turned into an eel; the Suqe men dragged it up to roast. Only the lame man, warned by the eel's eye, refused to eat — and as the great men bit, their legs turned to eels, then their bodies, and the whole club glided away into the water after its chief.
summary.zh: 一婦人浸於水中備織席之露兜葉，晨起取葉，葉已化鰻。蘇蓋會社諸人聞訊，以繩縛鰻曳回村中；會所旁的跛子不能同去，目睹鰻尾捲住克羅頓樹。鰻低語跛子：『他們吃時你莫吃。』眾人烤鰻於蘇蓋爐中；大人物一聲令下，人人下箸——一口咬下，腿化鰻；再咬，身化鰻；三咬，人人皆鰻，隨大人物滑入水中而去。

passages.text: A woman went to lay pandanus leaves to weave mats with in the water, and she laid them there in the evening and went home. In the morning she went to take the leaves from the water; and when she went to take them out, behold, they were turned into an eel. Then she ran back and told it to some men who were engaged in the suqe, and they ran down and tied a cord to the eel and dragged it up to the village. But there was a lame man who could not go with them, and he lay in the gamal, the club-house; and by the side of the gamal there was a croton-tree; and as they dragged up that eel it curled its tail round the croton, and the croton was nearly broken, and the lame man saw it. But they dragged hard at the eel and it loosed its tail from the croton, and they brought it into the village, and laid it at the entrance of the gamal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: So when they ran off for fire-wood and banana leaves to cook it with, the eel said to the lame man, 'When they are eating don't you eat; they shall eat by themselves.' Consequently the lame man did not eat; but they put the eel to be cooked in the oven of the suqe, and covered in the oven. And when they opened the oven they all took up pieces of the eel, every one of them a piece, and when the great man said to them, 'Now put them ready,' then they all put them ready; and after that he said again, 'Now let us eat,' and they all took a bite at once. But as they bit once their legs turned into eels; and they bit a second time and the bodies of them all turned into eels; and they bit again, and they were all eels; and the great man glided away first, and they all followed him into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Little Owl Who Became a Husband

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Two women gathering firewood found a young owl with white feathers and very large eyes; one day it was a man, and they took him into the village and he became their husband. When he took to beating them they reminded him — 'you are a bird, and our property because we found you' — and when they blew up the fire against his ban, he turned back into a bird and flew away, throwing money down to them as he went.
summary.zh: 兩名拾柴女子拾得一隻白羽大眼之幼鴞，養於家中；一日去看，小鳥已化作男子。二女攜他回村，他便做了她們的丈夫。三人相安多年，蓋屋耕園；後來他動輒毆打她們，她們斥道：『你是鳥，是我們拾來的財物，憑什麼打我們？』他揚言離去；晚間他飲下卡瓦，嚴禁二女撥火；她們偏把火撥旺照他——他登時化回鳥身，展翅而去，一路把錢拋給她們。

passages.text: This is about two women who were getting fire-wood, and found a young owl, a bird with white feathers and very large eyes; it was a young bird of this kind that they found. And one day the two women went to look at their little bird, and found that he was turned into a man; so they took him into the village, and he became their husband. And the three lived always in perfect harmony together, and built their house, and worked in their garden, and so remained many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: But after that he took to beating them when they quarrelled, and they scolded him for it, saying, 'You there are a bird, and our property because we found you; why do you beat us like this?' So he said he would leave them; and in the evening he drank kava, and forbade them to blow the fire. But when he lay down to sleep the two women blew up the fire into a blaze, and looked at him, and he turned into a bird, and flew away. And the two women cried after him, and he threw down money to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Betawerai and Walolo: The Banyan of Snakes
title.zh: 貝塔維賴與瓦洛洛：蛇榕誅滅記

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A boy kept a little red snake in a hollow yaqava trunk and fed it till it grew monstrous, ate him, and devoured the whole village — all but a pregnant woman who dug a pit and lived under a flat stone with her newborn twins. The serpent brood filled a banyan, chief among them Betawerai the branch-lord and Walolo the man-hunter; the twins grew, made bows, pelted the banyan, sang Walolo home end-over-end like a stick, and shot the snakes dead — burning the heap as a sign that the devouring snake was destroyed.
summary.zh: 一男孩執意收養一條小紅蛇，藏於空心亞瓜瓦樹幹中，以鼠、鳥、黑蜥、豬肉飼之；蛇漸成巨怪，一日搶食其豬，竟把男孩也吞了，出樹入村，把全村人吃盡。唯有一名孕婦掘地穴、以薄石板覆頂藏身，在穴中產下雙生子。巨蛇據榕而居，生下無數小蛇，為首者二：一為貝塔維賴，不能遠行，常駐榕枝（其名即取自大枝『貝塔』）；一為瓦洛洛，渡海獵人為食。雙子長成，求母製弓箭，往誅群蛇。二人以棒端翻擲擊榕，蛇紛紛墜地；貝塔維賴唱歌召瓦洛洛速歸殺敵——瓦洛洛聞歌，如木棍般一翻一翻地趕回；雙子輪番發箭，直至射斃瓦洛洛，再拉下貝塔維賴誅之。眾蛇堆於榕根，堆薪焚之，以為滅蛇之證；母子三人重返村中安居。

passages.text: The beginning was in this way; a woman and her child went to strip pandanus leaves for weaving mats, and the boy saw a young snake on the stalk of a leaf and begged his mother to let him have it, for he wanted it; his mother forbade him to take it. But he said that he wished for it, and so he laid hold on the little red snake, and took it and put it in the hollow trunk of a tree; and the name of that tree is the yaqava; he put it into the hollow of that, and he used to feed it with rats or birds or black lizards, or pig's flesh, and that snake became extremely large.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: And one day when he killed a pig he went to give it some; but that snake snatched the pig from him, and ate him up also, and crawled out of the hollow tree, and came into the village and ate up all the people in the place. But there was one pregnant woman who survived; and she dug a pit, and took a thin flat stone and laid it over the pit, and she stayed within it. And she brought forth her children, twins, and they three remained in that pit in the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the snake ate up all the people, and then went and took up its abode on a banyan-tree, and brought forth exceedingly many young ones, and two the chief among them. The name of one of these was Betawerai, and this one was not able to go about, but stayed always on a branch of the banyan — the branch of a big tree like a banyan they call a betavrai, like the flat of the hand, and this was named after that, At the branch. And the other one used to go very far away seeking diligently men or pigs to eat, and his name was Walolo. But one day those two, the children of the woman who had lived in the ground, begged of their mother to make them bows and arrows; and after that they said they would go into the village and seek that snake to shoot it and kill it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: And when they had gone and had seen from a distance that banyan where Betawerai and Walolo lived, they saw upon the branches, and on the little twigs, and on the leaves, nothing but snakes on that banyan. But Walolo was not on the tree, because he had gone across the sea and was still seeking for men to devour. And these two boys went up to the banyan-tree and began to pelt it with sticks thrown end over end; and while they were pelting so the snakes fell down in very great numbers. And Betawerai began to sing a song to make Walolo come quickly back and kill and eat them — 'Risuritu vano, Betawerai, a lang togalau, ti uvi goro nanagoiu, Walolo! Walolo! go vano mai! Turn and come to Betawerai, the wind is North-west, it blows against my face. Walolo, Walolo, come hither!' And they say that Walolo heard him singing, and came end over end like a stick; and as he came near, one of them shot him, and then the other shot, and both hit him; and they went on shooting like this, till they shot him to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Basi and the Snake Mother's Ten-Chambered House

region.en: Dama and Tanoriki, Maewo, Vanuatu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島達馬與塔諾里基（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Basi, daughter of a snake that lived in a cave at Dama, married Dovaowari of Tanoriki and begged leave for her mother to move near them — a house of ten chambers. On her arrival by night the earth quaked and thundered, and her tail coiled chamber by chamber till the whole house was snake, only a woman's head at the door. When her husband plotted to burn the house behind a dance, the snake warned Basi: 'if you see sparks run quickly back to me' — and both were burnt to death together; their liver remains, full of mana.
summary.zh: 達馬有女子巴希，其母為穴居之蛇。她嫁與塔諾里基青年多瓦奧瓦里；婚後她常回遠處探母，夫心不悅，遂允其母遷來同住。蛇母自慮身軀巨大，命女婿建一座十室之屋。遷居之夜，地動雷鳴，如世界將盡；蛇尾先入第一室，盤曲而進，直至十室盡滿，僅一顆人首向門而臥。晨起村人來看，方見是條人首巨蛇。蛇母又吞食門前豬雞；夫深惡之，藉遠村赴舞之機，囑人縱火焚屋滅蛇。蛇母早知其謀，囑巴希：『宴舞時若見火星迸出，速跑回來與我同死。』巴希舞中見火星四散，奔回縱身火中——母女俱焚。其肝存留至今，滿蓄瑪那。

sensitivity.note: Missionary-era record (Codrington 1891); Maewo heritage. Records a war/love-charm relic cult.

passages.text: She was a girl of Dama, and her mother, a snake, lived in a cave there. And there was a young man living at Tanoriki; and one day Basi and another girl went down to the beach to dip salt-water; and Dovaowari was the name of the youth, and he also went down to bathe in the sea, but on another part of the beach. These two girls stood looking over to the other part of the beach, and saw the fellow bathing, and washing his hair till it was exceedingly white; and they say, 'Let us two go and see who that is bathing.' And they went and saw that it was Dovaowari; and Basi said to the other girl, 'You go home to our mother, and tell her that I am going after Dovaowari.' But Dovaowari forbade her in vain to follow him, saying that he was poor, that he had no property and no garden; and she disputed with him, saying that she would certainly go with him. So they married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Basi kept going to her mother at Dama a long way off, and Dovao was vexed at it, and he told Basi to go and say to her mother that she was to move to that place so that all might live together. But the chief thing she thought of was how she should manage, because she was a snake very long and large, and if a small house were built for her it would not be enough. She considered, therefore, and said to Basi, 'Go and tell my son-in-law to build me a house, and let there be ten chambers in it.' But Dovao did not yet know the truth, and when he heard about the house with ten chambers he was astonished at it. When the house was finished, Basi carried the news, saying, 'Your house is finished'; but she had said beforehand, 'I shall go in the night, and if my son-in-law should hear anything don't let him take notice of it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: So in the middle of the night they heard an earthquake, and thunder, and a very great rumbling as if all the world would come to an end; and when she reached that place, her tail entered first and coiled itself in the first chamber, and then in the second, until all those chambers were filled with the big snake; and her head, a woman's, lay opposite the door, though the whole house was full of the snake. In the morning the people came to see this person, and saw that it was a snake with a human head. And whenever Dovao and Basi went anywhere and returned, she would go to her mother, that snake, and rub her nose upon her; but her husband did not like that sort of thing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the snake knew this, and called Basi and told her that they were going to set fire upon her and burn her that night, and, 'When you are standing at the feast, if you see sparks run quickly back to me.' So it was done; while she was dancing she saw sparks flying and ran quickly back and leapt herself into the fire, and both were burnt to death. And after a long while the liver that was burnt was found, and still remains, the liver of Basi and of her mother; and I have seen a bone in possession of some wealthy people; there is mana, magic power, in it, they say, for pigs, and for wicked intercourse with women when they blacken their faces under the eyes with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Deitari, the Boy Made of Tari's Blood
title.zh: 迪塔里：塔里血所生之子

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Tari cut himself in his garden, and set the blood by his fire-place in a bamboo vessel. Food began cooking itself; his wife spied out a boy, exceedingly fair, creeping from the bamboo — Deitari, Tari's blood. When the fish-man Taepupuliti changed himself into a fish and devoured the boy, Tari sent every fish and bird to search, until a little fish, extremely thin, found him hidden at the back of Taepupuliti's house — and a shared bowl of kava, which struck the eater of the child and not the father, let Tari carry his son home again.
summary.zh: 塔里在園中勞作時被劃傷，將血收入竹筒，置於灶邊。此後屢屢回家便有熟食等他，妻不知何人所備；她依夫言窺伺，見竹筒中爬出一個異常俊美的男孩——迪塔里，塔里之血所生。塔里夫婦大喜，視如己出。村童結伴浴於溪中唱歌，迪塔里亦往；有一名為 Taepupuliti 者，化身為魚，把這竹筒所出之童吞下，攜往他鄉。塔里遣盡百魚百鳥四出尋子，終由一條極瘦小魚尋得：孩子就藏在 Taepupuliti 屋後。塔里與其人共飲卡瓦，故意讓酒從口中漏出，使藥力不上身；而吞童者藥力大作，塔里遂把孩子又背了回去。

passages.text: They say that Tari went into his garden to work, and as he was working something cut him, and he put the blood into a bamboo vessel, and went into the village, and set it by his fire-place, and there it stayed. And after many days when he was going to work he told his wife to cook some food for him, and she went to get it. But when she came back into the house she found food already cooked, and she did not know who had prepared the food for her. Thus it happened very often, and the woman told her husband. And he when he heard it bade her sit and watch who it was that did it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: So she sat by the side wall of the house, and saw Deitari (Tari's Blood) creep out of the bamboo vessel which Tari had put aside; and she saw that he was exceedingly fair, and she hid him. Then when Tari came in from work he asked his wife, 'Haven't you seen him?' And she said, 'What was that you put by the fire-place?' Then he remembered about his blood, and he said to his wife, 'My blood was in that bamboo; and his wife said, 'I saw him come out of that bamboo that you had put there.' So she brought him forth, and Tari rejoiced very much to see him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: And one day as they were living together the boys of the village, and Deitari with them, went to bathe in the stream, and sang songs. And there was a man called Taepupuliti, and they say that he changed himself into a fish, and went and devoured the boy who had come out of the bamboo, and went off with him into a different country. And Tari sent every kind of fish and bird to seek for Deitari; and he found a little fish, extremely thin, and this fish and Deitari's father found him hidden at the back end of Taepupuliti's house. And they two, Tari and Taepupuliti, sat down to drink kava; and the father of the one whom the other had devoured let the liquor fall from his mouth as he drank, so that the kava did not strike (affect) him: but as for the one who had eaten his child it struck him very much, and his father carried him off again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖自馬埃沃至安巴埃（奧帕）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Tarkeke, a man-eater of all the islands, wove himself an image of a fish with vines and turned into it. His son, curious at his father's forbidden inner room, got into the image; a kingfisher's cry, a broken stick — and the fish with the boy inside crossed to Opa. The father followed in a rough netting on his breast, rescued the boy, then taught him his trade: 'Go, for you want to eat a man' — and the sea rose up the shore after his son, carrying him into the bread-fruit-tree and swallowing the man there. Laid at the back of the house, the boy saw the sea, the shark, the fishes with their mouths open, and died.
summary.zh: 塔爾克凱在各島間食人。他以藤蔓編成魚形，鑽入其中便化作魚，欲食人則游往奧帕或拉加。一日他外出去園中，其子擅入屋內禁地，鑽進那藤魚之中；翠鳥飛落屋頂為號，屋中老嫗聞聲折斷柴枝，藤魚便載著孩子下海，渡往奧帕。父親聞聲狂奔而回，已來不及，便取椰纖胡亂編物縛於胸前，下海尋子；至奧帕救回孩子——奧帕人幾乎把他射死。歸途見一人立於麵包樹上，父親對兒子說：『去，吃了他。』兒子答：『父親，他在陸上，我怎麼去？』父親斥責，他只得前去；海水竟隨他漲上沙灘，把他連人帶上樹，吞下那人。孩子被抬回屋後安置，他一動，便看見海、看見鯊、看見張口待食的群魚——就這樣在那裡死去了。

passages.text: They say that he used to devour men in all the islands, and that he made the image of a fish with woven vines, and got into it and turned into a fish. And when he wanted to eat a man he entered into that fish and went to Opa or Raga. One day he went into his garden, and his son was in the village, and his father had forbidden the boy to go to the inner part of the house; but his father had gone away and he and his mother were in the village, and he was playing about alone, and he thought he would go and see what it was that his father had forbidden him to see. So he went into the further end of the house, and saw the image of the fish lying, and got into it. And a kingfisher flies down as a sign if any one gets into the figure of the fish; and the old woman lying in the house when she hears the kingfisher breaks a stick, and the image then goes into the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: And when the boy got into the figure of the fish, and the kingfisher flew down to the roof of the house, and the old woman heard it, she broke a piece of fire-wood, and the image of the fish with the boy inside it went down into the sea, and crossed to Opa. And the father was in his garden and he heard a noise, and he ran as fast as he could, but found that the fish was already gone. So he weaves together the stuff that is on a cocoa-nut, in no particular shape, and puts it on his breast, and goes into the sea to seek the boy. And he finds him at Opa; and the Opa people, they say, had very nearly shot him. And his father brought him home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: And as they were coming back they saw a man in a bread-fruit-tree, and the father said to his son, 'Go and eat him'; and the son said to his father, 'How shall I go, father, because he is on dry land?' And his father hit him hard, and said, 'Go, for you want to eat a man.' Then he went, and as he went up towards the shore the sea went up too upon the shore, and he was carried up into the bread-fruit-tree after that man and swallowed him. And they came back to the back part of the house, and put him there, for he was not yet dead. And when they put him there at the further end of the house, and he moved himself about, he saw the sea, and the shark, and the fishes with their mouths open to devour him. And so he stayed there and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Widow and the Ghost Who Ate the Torch

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖馬埃沃島（奧羅拉島）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: A widow with a child at her hip met a ghost she took for her husband. Torching for fish by the shore, she left the child with him — and the ghost ate a finger, then the whole child, then ran to eat the mother, eating the coconut branches she had planted instead of her; she fled up a pandanus-tree and pelted him with fruit till dawn, when she saw him turn into a hermit crab.
summary.zh: 一名寡婦攜幼兒尋夫，途中遇一鬼，誤認為夫。三人同往海邊持炬照魚；婦人燃炬，鬼抱孩子，先咬去其一小指；婦人問，鬼答『蚊蟲叮的』。孩子止哭——鬼已把孩子整個吃掉。婦人這才確知遇鬼：她早沿岸插下椰枝作記，鬼食畢孩子便撲向她，慌亂中竟把那些椰枝一一吃掉，以為那就是她。婦人奔逃，攀上露兜樹；鬼欲攀樹食她，她便用樹果砸他，如此直到天明——晨光中她看見那鬼化作一隻寄居蟹。

passages.text: This is about a woman who lost her husband, and went in search of him, and she had a child with her. And a ghost met the woman carrying the child on her hip, and the woman thought it was her husband. And the three went down to the beach to burn for fish. Then the ghost said to the woman, 'You go and burn for fish, and I will look after our child.' And when the woman went with the torch the ghost ate one finger of the child. And its mother asked him what hurt the child, and the ghost said, 'Nothing, a mosquito bit it.' After he had spoken the child ceased to cry, and the woman discovered that it was a ghost because it had eaten the child entirely up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she knew for certain that it was a ghost, because she had set up cocoa-nut branches along the shore, and the ghost when it had eaten the child went to eat the mother, and as he ran along to eat her he ate the branches she had set up, thinking that the branches were the woman. And the woman ran away fast and climbed into a pandanus-tree, and when the ghost would have climbed up to eat her the woman pelted him down with the fruits. And so she did till dawn; and when it was light she saw that he turned into a hermit crab.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagaro the Little and the Conch-Shell Blast

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Night-caught on a lone gaviga-tree, Tagaro-mbiti listened as Merambuto and his brothers claimed branch after branch below him. Asked what was in his hand, he answered, 'The voice of you and me to be sure' — and promised to let them hear it from his cave. He slipped away, whistled his signal, and blew the conch with all his strength: the brothers fell from the tree and died, Merambuto leapt for joy till the rock of his cave stuck fast in his head and he died too; bushes grew where the brothers fell.
summary.zh: 小塔加羅訪 Vagimbangga 購豬，歸途天黑，遂攀一株孤零零的 gaviga 樹，食果而眠，手中握著法螺。夜半，默蘭布托與其兄弟們一路喧嚷而來，各自攀枝分佔，口稱『這是我的枝！』；默蘭布托攀至樹頂，撞見小塔加羅，問他手中何物。小塔加羅答：『正是你我二人的聲音。』並許諾：『先回去，你聽見我吹哨，便用這法螺說話給我聽。』他下樓騙過眾兄弟，回至洞府吹哨為號；小塔加羅聞哨，鼓足全力猛吹法螺——默蘭布托的兄弟們從樹上紛紛跌落而死；默蘭布托自己高興得在洞裡一次次跳起，頭撞洞頂岩石，岩石嵌進頭裡，也就死了。兄弟墜落之處，後來長出了灌木。小塔加羅天明回家。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage.

passages.text: They say that he went to a part of the island called Vagimbangga to pay for a pig there, and that on his return the sun set while he was still in the forest. And he was hungry, for he had nothing whatever to eat. Now beside that path they say there was a single gaviga-tree, with many branches, and also ripe fruit on it; and he climbed up to eat, and to sleep awhile on that tree; and in his hand was his conch-shell trumpet to blow as he went along the path. And in the middle of the night, when he had finished eating, he climbed further up to the top of that gaviga-tree to sleep and rest there; and as he begins to fall asleep he hears the voices of a number of people coming along underneath the gaviga-tree. And he woke up thinking that it was probably his brothers looking for him; but it was not so — these were Merambuto and his brothers coming along, and they climbed up the gaviga-tree themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Tagaro-mbiti sits perfectly still lest they should see him, and he hears one of them say 'Ineu ranganggu ngaha' — This is my branch — and so say all of them. Then says Merambuto, 'Ineu ranganggu ngaha lo vuhungegi' — This is my branch at the top — and this he said with a loud voice. And Merambuto climbed straight up to the top of that gaviga-tree, and there he found Tagaro-mbiti. Then says Merambuto, 'Who are you?' And says he, 'I am Tagaro-mbiti.' And he asked Tagaro again, 'What is that in your hand?' And he says, 'The voice of you and me to be sure.' And he begged of him to speak in that conch that he might hear it; but he said also, 'Wait a bit till I go back to my dwelling-place, and when I get there you will hear me whistle; then you shall speak with the voice of us two that I may hear it for myself.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: And he made haste down from the tree, and his brothers said, 'Are we to come too?' 'No,' says he, 'I am only going to get rid of a mess and then I shall come back.' Thus he deceived them; and when he reached his dwelling, the cave, he whistled for Tagaro to hear, that he might blow the conch. And Tagaro heard Merambuto whistle, and he put forth all his strength to blow the conch hard, and he blew, and Merambuto's brothers fell every one of them from the tree; and he himself was delighted and jumped high again and again in his cave, and his head struck against the rock, and the rock stuck fast into his head, and there he died. And his brothers who had fallen down died every one; and on that account they say that bushes grew up in that place where Merambuto's brothers fell. And when it was light Tagaro-mbiti returned to his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

region.zh: 瓦努阿圖麻瘋島（安巴埃）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Oral tradition; recorded by R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians, 1891, ch. XIX (native manuscript)

source.work: R. H. Codrington, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), ch. XIX 'Stories'

summary.en: Merambuto fed Tagaro badly, so Tagaro wrapped and threw away the food; then fed him on grated barrow-pig — and Merambuto grated up his own barrow-pig; then on meat he claimed was his mother cooked in the oven — and Merambuto cooked his mother in the oven. Then came the fire: 'Light a fire over me,' said Tagaro, who had dug a hole and survived his own burning; Merambuto asked for his turn, and Tagaro burned him up.
summary.zh: 默蘭布托請塔加羅吃飯，飯卻極差；塔加羅把食物包起偷偷扔掉，回請時端出擦絲閹豬肉。默蘭布托追問吃的是什麼，塔加羅答『擦絲的閹豬』，他便回家把自己的閹豬擦成絲。再問時塔加羅答得厭煩，騙他道：『我母親；我把她煮在爐裡了。』默蘭布托便回家把母親煮進爐中。塔加羅又說：『在我屋上放火吧。』默蘭布托紮緊門縱火；塔加羅在火中哀哭，默蘭布托笑他：『莫哭，你從前騙我，如今就要死了。』他以為塔加羅已死——其實塔加羅早掘好地洞藏身。翌晨默蘭布托來看，塔加羅安坐如常。默蘭布托說：『該我了，今夜你燒我的屋。』塔加羅縱火，把他燒了個乾淨。

sensitivity.note: Native manuscript translated by Codrington (1891); Aoba heritage. Cross-ref melanesian-tagaro-burning-house (Dixon recension).

passages.text: Merambuto prepared food for himself, and then he invited Tagaro to come that they might eat together. So Tagaro came to him in his house; and the food of Merambuto was exceedingly bad, and as they ate Tagaro did not eat at all, but he wrapped the food up to deceive Merambuto, and went and threw it away, and then went back to his house. Afterwards Tagaro sent after him saying, 'Merambuto, come here to my house.' Merambuto came and they two ate. And the food was good; Merambuto liked Tagaro's food very much; he had made his own not at all good. So Merambuto considered silently, 'What sort of thing is this we two are eating?' So he asked Tagaro, and Tagaro said to him, 'I have grated up my barrow pig.' So Merambuto went and grated up his barrow-pig, and in due course they two ate it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.

passages.text: After this Tagaro invited Merambuto to eat with him in return in his house. So he asked him again, 'What food is this we two are eating?' And Tagaro was tired of being asked, and deceived Merambuto, saying to him, 'My mother; I cooked her in the oven.' So Merambuto went home and cooked his mother in the oven. After this Tagaro said to him, 'Light a fire over me.' So Merambuto came, and tied up the door of Tagaro's house, bound it very tight, and set fire to Tagaro's house. Then Tagaro wept; Merambuto said to him, 'Don't cry, you deceived me formerly, now you are soon to die for it.' He thought that Tagaro was dead; but not at all, he had dug a hole, and stayed in it. In the morning thinking that he was dead he came, and Tagaro had been long sitting ready for him. So Merambuto asked him, 'Are you sitting like this?' Tagaro said, 'Yes.' So Merambuto said to him, 'My turn now, to-night you set fire to my house.' So Tagaro set fire to his house, and the fire burnt him up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Codrington, The Melanesians, ch. XIX (1891), native manuscript; not verbatim.
